docs.avatars.component: THE PEOPLE AT THE DESK, DRAWN ON IT — and where they sit is their own camera.
Every live page before this one shows what a hand is DOING and nothing about the person doing
it: the cursor appears while they move and is gone the moment they stop, so a desk with a quiet
second player reads as a desk with one player at it. Presence is the permanent half of that
message — who is here, what they are called, whether they are still looking, and where they sit.
Nothing else on a shared desk answers the last one. A seat number is something the game invented,
and a game with none would have no answer at all; how somebody turned, moved and zoomed their
view IS the direction they are looking at the desk from. So the place is read out of the view,
with the same arithmetic on every screen — which is why the message carries a view and never a
position: a position would be true on one glass and nowhere else.
An avatar is a NODE on the felt and not a badge over the glass — the seat design's disc: the
initials in the seat's ink, a cone of the look from its centre, the name on a plate under it, a
ring while the hand is full. Looking at their own place, it sits IN the arch of their chair
(`Live/Place`); looking elsewhere, it stands under their glass. A thing on the desk can become a
crocodile by having a different picture, and a rectangle drawn over the glass can become none of them.
docs.avatars.scene: AVATARS — one desk, two people, and each of them visible to the other.
Pan the top screen and its own disc leaves its chair and travels the felt with the view: a person
STANDS WHERE THEY ARE LOOKING, so the disc is the patch of felt under the low middle of that
reader's glass. On the bottom screen it moves exactly as far as the view did, which is the message
being sent: 'I am looking over here now'. Tap your own chair and the view glides home: the disc
sits back down in the arch.
The state is on the disc. Switch to another tab and both discs lose their cone — the tab is the
person, and a tab nobody is looking at is a person who is not looking at the desk. Pick anything
up and the holder's disc takes a ring, which is the one thing everybody else is waiting on.
The disc is never lifted, not even one's own: a picture of where a person is looking is a
reading, and a finger that moved it would be moving a measurement. To sit elsewhere, move your
CHAIR — the view, and with it the disc, comes back to it.
NO SERVER. The two screens are two views of one tree, exactly as on the pages before this one,
and the presence travels the same seam a hand does.
